video_metadata.working_title: TEXAS 2010 Mystery Identified After 6 Years — The Woman Who Lived as Lori Ruff
video_metadata.topic_one_sentence: A Longview, Texas mother who died by suicide on Christmas Eve 2010 left a locked box proving she had built her adult life on the birth certificate of a toddler who died in a 1971 fire, and it took a Social Security investigator, a Seattle Times reporter, a forensic genealogist and consumer DNA until September 2016 to give her back her real name: Kimberly McLean of the Philadelphia area, who had left home in 1986.
video_metadata.primary_emotion_to_evoke: haunted curiosity turning into compassion: the mystery of a hidden life, and the grief of three families (the Ruffs, the Turners, the McLeans)

protagonist._instructions: The main character of your story - can be hero, villain, or antihero. Fill with verified facts only.
protagonist.full_name: Born Kimberly Maria McLean; lived from 1988 as Lori Erica Kennedy, and from her 2004 marriage as Lori Erica Ruff. Before the Dallas name change she briefly held documents in the name Becky Sue Turner.
protagonist.age_at_time_of_events: About 17 or 18 when she left home in 1986 (sources differ); about 19-20 when she built the new identity in 1988; in her early forties when she died on December 24, 2010. Exact birth date not reliably established for publication: the obituary gives July 18, 1969 (the date she used as Lori); Wikipedia gives a 1968 date for Kimberly McLean.
protagonist.occupation_or_status: Graduate of the University of Texas at Arlington (1997, Bachelor in Business, marketing concentration, per her obituary); wife of Blake Ruff from January 2004; mother of one daughter born in 2008; lived in Longview, Texas.
protagonist.location: Philadelphia area, Pennsylvania (childhood); Dallas area, Texas (from 1988); Longview, Texas (married life and death).
protagonist.physical_description: Not used beyond what her real published photos show (driver's license and family photos released by the Seattle Times).
protagonist.background_brief: Born in Philadelphia to James and Deanne McLean (nee Cassidy). After her parents divorced, her mother gained custody of Kimberly and her sister, married a second husband, Robert Becker, and moved the family (Wikipedia names Wyncote; Fox News/Seattle Times say her mother's King of Prussia home). Kimberly left home in 1986. In 1988 she obtained the birth certificate of Becky Sue Turner, a toddler who died in a 1971 house fire in Fife, Washington, used it to get an Idaho ID card (June 16, 1988), and changed that name in a Dallas court to Lori Erica Kennedy (July 5, 1988), then obtained a Social Security number and Texas documents as Lori Kennedy. Wikipedia places the McLean-Cassidy family on the Philadelphia Main Line.
protagonist.psychological_profile: Documented only through behaviour reported by the Seattle Times and secondary outlets: guarded and evasive about her past; told her husband's family her parents were dead and she had no siblings; after her daughter's birth in 2008 sometimes kept the girl away from Blake's family; the marriage broke down in 2010. No diagnosis is public; the script must not speculate about mental illness.
protagonist.mundane_humanizing_detail: She went back to school and earned a business degree with a marketing concentration at the University of Texas at Arlington in 1997, nine years after taking her new name.
protagonist.nickname_or_alias_if_any: Becky Sue Turner (stolen identity, 1988); Lori Erica Kennedy (legal name from July 5, 1988); Lori Erica Ruff (married name); 'Jane Doe' (how investigator Joe Velling referred to her).

victims_or_targets._instructions: People affected by the protagonist's actions. Include 3-5 key figures minimum.

individuals.name: Becky Sue Turner
individuals.connection_to_protagonist: Her birth certificate was requested in Bakersfield and used in 1988 to build the identity that became Lori Erica Kennedy.
individuals.specific_impact_suffered: She died at age 2 in a house fire in Fife, Washington, in 1971; seventeen years later her name was borrowed by a stranger.
individuals.humanizing_detail: She never reached her third birthday. Her family is not quoted in available sources.

individuals.name: Blake Ruff (Jon Blakeley Ruff)
individuals.role_or_profession: Husband of Lori Ruff, of Longview, Texas
individuals.connection_to_protagonist: Married her in January 2004; father of her daughter; moved to his parents' home and filed for divorce in 2010.
individuals.specific_impact_suffered: Learned after her death that he had never known his wife's real name.
individuals.humanizing_detail: Sought marriage counseling before seeking a divorce (secondary sources).

individuals.name: The Ruff family (Blake's parents, Nancy and Jon Ruff, of Longview)
individuals.connection_to_protagonist: She died in their driveway on December 24, 2010; they and Blake found and opened the locked box.
individuals.specific_impact_suffered: Years of unanswered questions; they sought help from public officials (a congressman's aide brought the case to investigator Joe Velling).
individuals.humanizing_detail: Named in her obituary as her in-laws in Longview.

individuals.name: The daughter [MENOR]
individuals.role_or_profession: Child of Lori and Blake Ruff, born 2008
individuals.connection_to_protagonist: Her DNA, together with her father's, later allowed genealogists to isolate her mother's genetic family.
individuals.specific_impact_suffered: Lost her mother at about two years old.
individuals.humanizing_detail: Not named in the script; she was a minor.

individuals.name: The McLean and Cassidy families of the Philadelphia area
individuals.connection_to_protagonist: Last saw Kimberly in 1986; identified her from her Texas driver's license photo in March 2016.
individuals.specific_impact_suffered: About 30 years without knowing where she was.
individuals.humanizing_detail: A relative recognized her instantly: 'My God, that's Kimberly!'
individuals.any_quotes_from_them: 'My God, that's Kimberly!' (Cassidy family member, as reported by the Seattle Times, relayed by Fox News and Mental Floss)

collective_victims_if_applicable.group_description: Three families touched by one hidden identity: the Turners (whose dead child's name was used), the Ruffs (who married into a stranger's secret), and the McLeans/Cassidys (who lost a daughter to silence).
collective_victims_if_applicable.range_of_impacts: Grief, confusion, years of unanswered questions.

supporting_characters._instructions: Investigators, accomplices, witnesses, family members - anyone who plays a significant role.

characters.name: Joe (Joseph) Velling
characters.role_in_story: Social Security Administration investigator based in Seattle (described as 'former' SSA investigator by 2016).
characters.key_actions_they_took: Received the case around 2011 after a congressman's aide asked him to look at it; reconstructed the 1988 paper trail; worked it for years; flew to Philadelphia in March 2016 and showed Lori's driver's license photo to a member of the Cassidy family.
characters.notable_quotes: No verified direct quote located. He called her 'Jane Doe' (Fox News 2016 paraphrase).

characters.name: Maureen O'Hagan
characters.role_in_story: Seattle Times reporter who wrote the June 2013 feature and the 2016 follow-up; later author of the audiobook 'The Woman in the Strongbox'.
characters.key_actions_they_took: Published the story and photos of the clues online and asked readers for help, which sparked worldwide interest and drew Colleen Fitzpatrick in.
characters.notable_quotes: 'So far, we've gotten a lot of response, but they haven't cracked the case yet.' (email to Poynter, June 2013)

characters.name: Colleen M. Fitzpatrick
characters.key_actions_they_took: Talked with Velling from June 2013; using the DNA the Ruff family submitted and high-density SNP testing borrowed from the genetic genealogy community, found that Lori had a first cousin in the Cassidy family of Philadelphia (December 2015); presented the case at the American Academy of Forensic Sciences in 2017.

characters.name: Uncle Tom (Deanne McLean's brother)
characters.role_in_story: Relative who described Kimberly's anger after her parents' separation.
characters.key_actions_they_took: Gave reporters background on Kimberly's teenage years.
characters.notable_quotes: Paraphrase only: Kimberly grew irate after her mother and father separated in the 1980s (Mental Floss).

characters.name: Online volunteers ('web sleuths')
characters.role_in_story: Crowdsourced readers who followed the case after 2013.
characters.key_actions_they_took: Analyzed the published clues; the user brief names the 'DNA Detectives' group, but no source located in this research ties that group specifically to the solution.

cold_open_material._instructions: The most dramatic moment of your story - this will be your hook.

the_moment.what_is_happening: A mother in her early forties, in the middle of a bitter divorce, dies by suicide in her car in her former in-laws' driveway on Christmas Eve. Afterwards her family opens a locked box from her closet.
the_moment.what_makes_it_shocking: Inside is the birth certificate of a two-year-old who died in a fire in Washington State in 1971, and papers showing the woman had changed that dead child's name to 'Lori Erica Kennedy' in a Dallas court in 1988.
the_moment.ironic_twist: She had a degree, a husband, a daughter, a Social Security number and a driver's license, and not one of them carried her real name.

cold_open_material.central_mystery_question: Who was the woman who lived for 22 years as Lori Erica Ruff, and why did she hide?

the_method._instructions: How did the protagonist do what they did? Technical details that can be explained to a general audience.
the_method.technique_name: Identity built on a deceased child's birth certificate, later solved with consumer autosomal DNA (genetic genealogy).
step_by_step_explanation: 1988: requested Becky Sue Turner's birth certificate from Bakersfield, California.
June 16, 1988: used it to get an Idaho ID card with her own photo.
July 5, 1988: changed the name legally in a Dallas court to Lori Erica Kennedy.
July 12-13, 1988: obtained a Social Security number and a Texas ID card as Lori Kennedy; April 1989 a Texas driver's license.

Solution: DNA from her husband and daughter was analyzed with direct-to-consumer autosomal SNP testing; by subtracting the father's side, the mother's relatives could be found; a first-cousin match pointed to the Cassidy family; a photo identification and further DNA tests confirmed it.
the_method.why_it_worked: In that era a birth certificate could be obtained for a child who had died in another state, because birth and death records were not systematically cross-checked across state lines (general context, stated as such). Once the name was changed in court, the dead child's name vanished from her later records.

technical_terms_to_explain.simple_explanation: The DNA we inherit from both parents, about half from each, which can reveal cousins as well as parents and siblings.
Reading hundreds of thousands of tiny single-letter spelling variations in the DNA, the same kind of test sold by consumer ancestry companies.
Two people sharing roughly the amount of DNA expected from sharing a set of grandparents.
The National Missing and Unidentified Persons System, a federal database where missing and unidentified cases are listed.

the_method.scale_of_operation: One person, one identity, held for 22 years (1988-2010).

systemic_failure._instructions: What institution, system, or authority failed to prevent this?
systemic_failure.institution_that_failed: Vital-records and identity-document systems of the 1980s (birth certificates, state ID cards, court name changes, Social Security numbers).
systemic_failure.how_they_were_supposed_to_protect: Identity documents are meant to confirm that a person is who they claim to be.
systemic_failure.why_they_failed: A birth certificate of a child who died in another state was issued and accepted; within a month it led to two state ID cards, a court-ordered name change and a Social Security number.
specific_incompetence_examples: June 16 to July 13, 1988: four official documents in 27 days built on a dead toddler's birth certificate.
No criminal case was ever brought; the identity was discovered only because the family opened her box after her death.
systemic_failure.ironic_details_about_the_failure: The Social Security number she obtained in 1988 is what later brought a Social Security investigator to the case, and even he could not find her real name with records alone.

the_investigation.investigating_agency: Social Security Administration (investigator Joe Velling, Seattle), with forensic genealogist Colleen Fitzpatrick and the Seattle Times.
the_investigation.initial_wrong_assumptions: No documented wrong suspects. Public speculation online after 2013 is not used.
the_investigation.key_breakthrough: December 2015: autosomal DNA from the husband and daughter revealed a first cousin in the Cassidy family of Philadelphia.
the_investigation.the_fatal_mistake: Not applicable (no crime prosecuted). The clue was the box she kept.
the_investigation.how_long_until_caught: Identified about five years and nine months after her death (Dec. 2010 to Sept. 2016), rounded as 'nearly six years'; about 28 years after the identity was created; about 30 years after she left home.

the_confrontation._instructions: The arrest, raid, or climactic moment when everything collapses.
the_confrontation.scene_description: Velling shows a member of the Cassidy family the Texas driver's license photo of Lori Ruff.
the_confrontation.ironic_or_absurd_details: The face on a 1989 Texas license, issued in the name of a dead child's replacement identity, was recognized in seconds by her own family.

legal_resolution.notable_court_testimony: None. The only court act in the story is the July 5, 1988 Dallas name change.
legal_resolution.sentence_received: None. She died before her identity was discovered and was never charged with any crime.
legal_resolution.current_status: As of October 2026: identification considered resolved since September 2016 (NamUs entry removed Sept. 19, 2016). No criminal case. Open questions remain: where she was between 1986 and 1988 and why she chose to hide.

universal_stakes.why_this_matters_to_viewer: It shows how a person can disappear inside paperwork, and how consumer DNA now makes it almost impossible to stay hidden from one's own family.
universal_stakes.how_this_could_happen_to_them: Anyone can marry, love and build a family with someone whose past they never truly know.
universal_stakes.lesson_or_warning: Behind every hidden identity are real families on both ends: the one left behind and the one never told.
universal_stakes.current_relevance: The case was solved in 2015-2016, just before genetic genealogy became famous through the Golden State Killer arrest in April 2018; it is an early example of the technique used to identify a person rather than a perpetrator.
